intro: Martial arts can be sorted into families: grappling, striking, armed as sport, flowing practice, diaspora and modern mix. Real bodies have drawn such lists, from the Japanese Budo Association in 1977 to UNESCO's heritage list. In this unit you will read those lists as records made by people, in given years, for their own purposes.

You will meet arts from Iceland, France, Japan, China, Trinidad, Israel and Switzerland. Glima went to the 1912 Stockholm Olympics as a demonstration. Kalinda survived a colonial law in 1884. Aikido chose to hold no contests, while fencing has been at every modern Olympic Games.

In the second chapter you will compare two sword sports, fencing and kendo, by origin, room, nation and code. You will use dated charters, federation records and rule books. By the end, you can build a comparison that explains differences with evidence and does not rank one art above another.
bigQuestion: How can a historian compare martial arts from different places fairly, using dated records instead of ranking them?

timeline.t: Charles IX grants letters patent to the fencing masters of Paris
Japan's Haitōrei bans most people from wearing swords in public
A colonial law in Trinidad restricts drumming and stick-fighting bands
Switzerland's federal wrestling association is founded
Icelanders demonstrate glima at the Stockholm Olympics
The International Fencing Federation (FIE) is founded in Paris
Olympic épée is scored electrically for the first time, in Berlin
The name aikido comes into official use
China publishes a simplified 24-movement taijiquan routine
Wheelchair fencing is part of the first Paralympic Games in Rome
The International Kendo Federation holds the first World Kendo Championships
Nine federations form the Japanese Budo Association

words.d: a group that people draw around things sharing a trait
a Japanese martial tradition, usually founded before 1868
modern Japanese budo arts organized after 1868
living practices that UNESCO lists for protection, such as games and rituals
an Olympic event shown without official medals
something built by joining parts of several older things
people scattered from a homeland, and the culture they carry or rebuild
an open royal document granting a right or status
a body that writes one set of rules for a sport across many countries
a permit showing that a person may take part in official events
a numbered advanced grade in Japanese arts, earned by examination in kendo
ordering things from better to worse by one standard

test.q: Which body formed in 1977 with nine Japanese federations?
test.why: Nine federations and the Nippon Budokan formed the Japanese Budo Association in 1977.

test.q: Which year did Donn Draeger use to divide classical from modern Japanese arts?
test.why: Draeger used the Meiji Restoration of 1868 as his working border.

test.q: Which practice was inscribed on UNESCO's list in 2020?
What happened to glima at the 1912 Olympics?
choices: It won Iceland a gold medal
It was shown as a demonstration
test.why: Icelanders demonstrated glima in Stockholm in 1912.

test.q: Which teacher blended English boxing with French kicking in the 1830s?
test.why: Charles Lecour studied English boxing and joined it with French kicking.

test.q: Which art is best described as a modern mix built for an army?
test.why: Imi Lichtenfeld built krav maga for Jewish defense groups and the Israel Defense Forces.

test.q: What equipment change in the 1700s made kendo contests possible?
test.why: The shinai and bogu allowed full-speed contests.

test.q: Why does aikido fit the flowing-practice family only in part?
choices: The Aikikai holds no contests, but Tomiki's branch does
test.why: Aikido has one room without contests and another with them.

test.q: Which family does kalinda belong to in this unit?
test.why: Kalinda grew among Africans and their descendants in Trinidad, a diaspora history.

test.q: What did King Charles IX grant in 1567?
choices: Letters patent to the Paris fencing masters
test.why: The 1567 letters patent let the Paris masters govern their trade.

test.q: In what language does the FIE give referee commands?
test.why: FIE rules give commands such as en garde and allez in French.

test.q: When was the International Kendo Federation founded?
test.why: The FIK was founded in 1970 and held the first World Kendo Championships that year.

test.q: Which weapon was scored electrically at the Olympics first?
test.why: Olympic épée used electric scoring first, at Berlin in 1936.

test.q: Where were the first Paralympic Games, with wheelchair fencing, held in 1960?
test.why: The first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960.

choices: Kendo is less modern than fencing
Fencing is the better sword sport
Fencing's world body dates from 1913 and kendo's from 1970
Sumo is more serious than schwingen
test.why: It sets two dated facts side by side and adds no judgment.

write.prompt: Compare two martial arts from this unit by origin, room, nation and code. Cite at least three dated records by name, such as the 1567 letters patent, the FIE's 1913 founding or the Haitōrei of 1876, and explain each difference without ranking.
tips: Name each record and its year, such as the All Japan Kendo Federation, 1952.
Use the same four questions for both arts: origin, room, nation, code.
Attribute beliefs to the people who hold them, such as Ueshiba's words about harmony.
Replace words like better or more advanced with a dated fact.
Use the unit's terms, such as category, federation, licence and diaspora.
